data.name: Painting to Gogh

audit.sub: Where the account is leaking and where the upside is. All figures Klaviyo-attributed unless noted; windows are the last 12 complete months through Jul 2026. This audit covers campaigns and the automation layer, since the two compound together.

wins.title: Turn clicks into orders
wins.detail: Opens are healthy at 52.6% and clicks are only modestly behind a comparable account, but placed-order rate (about 0.04% vs 0.09%) and revenue per email (about $0.03 vs $0.09) run two to three times behind. The money is in conversion after the click: the offer, the landing pages and the path to order, lifted with testing.

wins.title: Consolidate and lift the abandonment flows
wins.detail: Cart earns about $0.51 per email vs ~$1.73 and browse $0.30 vs $0.77, and both are split across many thin flows (browse alone is eight) that can never gather enough traffic to test. Consolidating each abandonment type into one flow with show-and-hide logic, then optimising, is the fastest flow gain.

wins.title: Use the off-season to test for peak
wins.detail: Revenue is structurally seasonal and cannot be flattened by pushing harder in the quiet months. Use the off-season to test offers, flows, the popup and creative so the winning playbook is locked in before the November-to-February peak. And build year-round gifting occasions, above all a birthday program that captures customers' and their loved ones' birthdays, to seed off-season demand the calendar otherwise starves.

wins.title: Build out the retention layer
wins.detail: The core flows are automated; the high-value retention flows are missing, win-back, sunset, VIP, replenishment, birthday, prospect nurture and back-in-stock. Adding them, on a giftable, repeat-purchase product, grows repeat revenue, conservatively about $60k a year.

wins.title: Pull down the flow unsub rate
wins.detail: Flow unsub runs about 0.6%, roughly double a healthy rate and double the campaign rate. Fixing the worst-offender early-sequence emails retains subscribers and protects future revenue.

wins.title: Make testing systematic
wins.detail: Testing has started, 2 flow tests live now, 6 flows tested, and the popup, but 27 of 34 flows and nearly all campaigns run untested. Putting every flow and the campaign calendar on a constant testing cadence turns each other fix in this audit into a compounding gain.

wins.title: Speed up abandonment re-entry
wins.detail: Abandonment flows earn about $203k a year, but a 30-day (or enter-once) re-entry lock means repeat abandoners, common on a multi-occasion gift product, get no reminder. Dropping re-entry to 4 to 7 days re-qualifies those sessions; a conservative 20 to 25% lift is about $45k a year, from a minutes-per-flow change.

wins.title: Recycle winning campaigns into the calendar
wins.detail: Within-season, the top fifth of campaigns earn about 2.2x their month and the bottom fifth 0.45x, and the winners are not reused. Building the quarterly calendar around proven concepts, refreshed, with a few new challengers to unseat them, lifts the average campaign over time.

audit.title: Account audit

findings.body: The store did about $5.96M over the last 12 months, but email and SMS drove only 20.3% of it. A well-run lifecycle and campaign program typically drives 25% to 35% of store revenue, often more. Lifting email from 20% to around 28% of store revenue, still only the middle of a healthy range, is worth roughly $460,000 in additional email revenue a year. Toggle the chart to 24 mo to see how sharply seasonal the store is; the wins below are how we close the gap and smooth it out.
findings.title: Email drives 20% of a $5.96M store

findings.body:
You segment by engagement and send most campaigns to the active core, which is exactly right and protects deliverability. Most accounts we audit blast everyone; you do not.

Where we would push further: tailor campaigns to the Want interest, with a bestseller block so people still discover other ranges.

chart.note: You concentrate most sends on the recently engaged core, which is good practice and keeps deliverability strong.
chart.freqHead: How often each engagement tier is mailed

findings.title: Your list targeting is already a real strength

findings.body: Opens are healthy at 52.6%, on par with our benchmark. But revenue per email runs about a third of a comparable account, so the gap is conversion after the click, the offer and the path to order, not opens or the list.

chart.note: Revenue per email vs a comparable account we manage.

findings.title: Healthy opens, but the clicks are not turning into orders

findings.body:
Ranked within-season, the top fifth of campaigns earn about twice their month's average and the bottom fifth about half. Founder voice, named launches, gift guides and plain-text win; generic blasts, minor holidays and gift-card pushes lose.

Reuse the winners, retire the losers, and build the calendar around what works.

live: Named product launches (a story, not a SKU)
chart.note: Ranked over 24 months against each campaign's own month, so this is the concept, not the timing. Sales and operational sends excluded.

Average revenue per campaign by concept, over 24 months (sales and operational sends excluded). Blue concepts out-earn the account's average campaign; red ones, generic Product Focus blasts, minor calendar holidays, one-off collections, run below it. The calendar play is simple: more of the blue, less of the red.

findings.title: The winning campaign concepts are clear, so lean into them

findings.body: Each flow's live message count against the depth our retention map recommends. The red counts are underbuilt, stopping too early; build those out first.
findings.title: Message depth vs our retention-map recommendation

findings.body:
The clean way to segment is the Want tag from the opt-in, which covers about 96% of subscribers. Over the last 120 days Date Night leads new signups (roughly 45 to 60%), with Individual climbing and Kids and Paint Party smaller.

Personalize the message by Want, and time Date Night around Valentine's, its peak season.

chart.note: Share of new opt-ins by declared Want across the last 120 days (oldest to newest). Capping at 120 days excludes the Valentine's acquisition spike: even so, Date Night stays the largest share (about 45 to 59%), while Individual climbs steadily toward ~28% in the most recent weeks. Hover for share and counts.

findings.title: Segment by declared intent (Want), led by Date Night

findings.body:
The cohorts are real, so personalize the message, but do not clone flows per cohort. Purchase collections cross-tag, so most buyers look like every cohort, and only about 7,900 people buy in 90 days, too thin to split and test.

One flow per trigger, personalized with dynamic blocks. Segment the message, not the machinery.

chart.note: Each bar is one abandonment type; the slices are its separate flows. Browse is split eight ways, checkout seven. The thin slices barely send: one checkout variant got 40 emails in a year, the site-abandon Triple Whale flow got two. Traffic this thin cannot reach significance, so none of it can be tested.

findings.title: Personalize by declared intent, but keep the flows consolidated

findings.body: Every abandonment flow re-opens only after 30 days, and some never re-open, when 4 to 7 days is right, so repeat abandoners get no reminder. One of the fastest, lowest-risk fixes in the account.
findings.title: Every abandonment flow re-opens too slowly, so repeat abandoners are missed

findings.body:
The core flows are all in place; the post-purchase retention layer is not. Missing: win-back (run by hand today), sunset, VIP, replenishment, birthday, prospect nurture and back-in-stock.

On a giftable, repeat-purchase product, this is the biggest build opportunity.

chart.note: The acquisition and pre-purchase flows are all present; the post-first-purchase retention layer is where the gaps are.

findings.title: Win-back is run by hand, and a whole retention layer is missing

findings.body:
Revenue swings hard: the store does roughly $700k to $1.4M a month through the gifting season, about November to February, then falls to around $175k to $234k in spring and summer.

This is a gifting brand, and that seasonality is largely structural. You will not flatten it by pushing harder on the same sends in the quiet months, and pretending otherwise wastes effort.

Two things help. First, treat the off-season as the lab: test relentlessly, the offers, the flows, the popup, the creative, so the winning playbook is locked in before the season hits, when every point of improvement is multiplied across the huge Q4-to-Valentine's volume. Second, and more structurally, manufacture gifting occasions that fall all year round, above all a birthday program (see the retention layer): by capturing customers' own birthdays and the birthdays of the people they buy for, the brand seeds a steady stream of off-season gift demand.

chart.note: Monthly store revenue. Gold bars are the November-to-February gifting peak; grey are the spring and summer trough. The swing is structural for a gifting brand.
chart.birthdayNote: Conservative estimate: about 3,000 birthday reminders a month (loved-ones' dates captured at opt-in and via a one-time list campaign) at a ~5% order rate on these high-intent, occasion-timed sends and a ~$79 average order, roughly $12k a month, about $144k a year of net-new revenue. Because it is flat across the calendar, it fills the off-season troughs proportionally more.

findings.title: Deeply seasonal, so the off-season is for testing, not forcing sales

findings.body:
Blended flow unsub reads about 0.6%, but that is SMS. Toggle Email vs SMS: email runs about 0.5% on flows and 0.27% on campaigns (healthy is 0.2 to 0.3%), while SMS runs about 3% on flows and 1.6% on campaigns. SMS is where the rate is high, as it tends to be.

Lever: tighten SMS cadence and consent, and fix a couple of worst-offender flow emails (expand below).
findings.title: Unsub rate is healthy on email, high on SMS

findings.body:
Capture works, about 5,700 email and 1,400 SMS opt-ins a month. The build is decent, but the offer is a weak 5% and the popup is badly under-tested, four tests in thirteen months on the highest-traffic asset.

Test a stronger offer and a cleaner, art-forward design.

chart.note: The four steps of the current mobile popup. The layout is busy and the discount competes with the artwork, when the artwork is what people are there for.

callouts.text: High-contrast CTA buttons stand out well
On the SMS step the consent disclaimer overlaps the images: hard to read and a compliance risk
Low-contrast email field against the busy background
Headline and body text overlap the photos in places
Test: if the order rate holds, reveal the discount on the question step with a Shop Now button, instead of forcing email first

Desktop bug: the Paint Party option on the first screen tags no one and closes the form (it works on mobile). A closed form does not reappear until the next day, and with no teaser bubble those visitors are simply lost.

findings.title: The popup works, but it is visually muddy and badly under-tested

findings.body:
Credit where due: A/B testing is happening. Two flow tests are running right now (the Kids and Paint Party welcome flows), four more flows have concluded tests, and the popup has been tested. A real habit is forming.

But it is thin: 27 of the 34 live flows have never been tested, and campaigns are rarely tested at all. Testing is the multiplier on every other fix in this audit, so the opportunity is to make it systematic, every flow and the whole campaign calendar on a constant cadence, not a handful of flows now and then.

chart.themSub: flows ever A/B tested (2 running now); campaigns rarely

findings.title: Testing has started, but it is thin and inconsistent

findings.body: Everything in this audit is day-to-day work for us: campaign strategy and segmentation, the automated flow architecture, SMS, list health, and relentless testing. None of it is overnight. We do the unglamorous work most people avoid, testing and building a little more every week so the gains compound. What you end up with is a retention system that is a beast: one that keeps earning in the quiet months and does not falter when the going gets tough. The wins at the top are the roadmap, and the figures are deliberately conservative and meant to be realised over time, not in a single month. Most of our clients sit between $3M and $20M in revenue, with the average around $5M to $8M. We build a package to fit.
findings.title: Where Zee.Media comes in
